blocks.name: Why CoDesign and when to engage
blocks.obj: Explain in two sentences what CoDesign is for and recognise the moments to bring the team in.
blocks.who: Everyone who meets clients: sales, account teams, BRMs (Business Relationship Managers), site and tech leads.
blocks.acc: Arnaud (business positioning).
blocks.when: Before any client conversation about experience, renewal or a new site.
blocks.inputs: Account situation: contract end date, satisfaction trend, planned site changes.
steps: Spot a trigger: contract ends in 18 months or less, a priority client must be retained, satisfaction is slipping, a new site or refurbishment is planned
Check sponsorship: a senior client sponsor, an account owner and a tech owner
Call the CoDesign team for a Presales conversation (02)
blocks.output: A qualified lead for 02 Presales.
blocks.std: Trigger and sponsor named.
blocks.quality: Engage early: 18 months before renewal works better than 2-3 months.
blocks.mistakes: Calling CoDesign for a one-off workshop at the last minute · no sponsor.
blocks.example: WORK: Northbridge restaurant contract renews in 16 months and attendance is flat → trigger met; sponsor = Head of Workplace. [fictional]

var.HEAL: Patient-experience scores falling two quarters in a row.

blocks.cred: Use named projects only; commercial figures need Arnaud's sign-off (see conflicts register).
blocks.prompt: Generic Claude prompt: 'Here is an account summary [paste]. Which CoDesign engagement triggers apply, and what 3 questions should I ask the client sponsor?'
blocks.verify: Contract dates and sponsor names.
blocks.fallback: The four-trigger checklist above.
blocks.l_obj: Identify an engagement trigger in an account description and name the sponsor needed.
blocks.explain: Clients don't renew a contract; they renew the experience they helped create. CoDesign brings users, frontline teams and sponsors into decisions early.

exercise.situation: Three account descriptions (one per segment pack).
questions: Which trigger applies?
Who must sponsor?
Is it too late, too early or right?

answer_key.sample_answer: Northbridge: 16 months, trigger met. Riverside: new stand, right time. St Aldric: falling scores, sponsor = director of patient experience.
answer_key.success_criteria: Trigger and sponsor correctly identified.

blocks.name: Team, roles and regional operating model
blocks.obj: Know who does what in an engagement and where regional colleagues contribute.
blocks.who: CoDesign core team (method, facilitation, templates) · regional champions and local designers (local cases, supported delivery) · account, sales and BRMs (access, sponsorship, continuity) · tech pre-sales (capability fit).
blocks.acc: Proposed ownership (to confirm): Diane integration · Noël method and quality · Gabriel templates, evidence, OS mapping · Arnaud positioning and sponsor review.
blocks.when: At every project start (03.01 RACI).
blocks.inputs: Project RACI; capability self-assessment.
steps: Find your role in the RACI
Check the capability level your role needs (N0-N4)
Agree supported tasks with the CoDesign lead
blocks.output: Your role and level for the engagement.
blocks.std: Every task has one accountable person.
blocks.quality: People act at the level they have shown, with coaching above it.
blocks.mistakes: Assuming attendance at training = independent delivery.
blocks.example: HEAL: on St Aldric the BRM Healthcare joins site visits as Contributor (N1) and co-facilitates one group (N2, coached). [fictional]

var.WORK: BRM Corporate co-hosts the Northbridge kick-off.

blocks.prompt: Planning & RACI agent with project scope and team list.
blocks.verify: Names and availability.
blocks.fallback: RACI table by hand.
blocks.l_obj: Place yourself in a RACI and state your target level.
blocks.explain: The method scales through documentation, tooling and people close to the business.

exercise.situation: RACI for a Format A workshop project.
questions: Which tasks are yours?
Which need coaching?
Who signs off?

answer_key.sample_answer: Depends on role; sign-off sits with CoDesign lead and client sponsor.
answer_key.success_criteria: Accountable person named per task.

blocks.name: End-to-end approach and the six-section campus
blocks.obj: Describe the end-to-end process: Presales, then the four Double Diamond phases.
blocks.who: All learners.
blocks.acc: Noël (method).
blocks.when: Start of any learning route.
blocks.inputs: This campus.
steps: 02 Presales: frame the opportunity, before the Double Diamond
03 Discover: diverge on the problem with evidence
04 Define: converge on who, what hurts, where to act
05 Co-create: diverge on solutions with users and client
06 Test & Deliver: converge on tested, owned decisions
blocks.output: Shared mental model.
blocks.std: Learner can place any activity in the right section.
blocks.quality: Six campus sections = one introduction + five process sections. Presales precedes the four Double Diamond phases.
blocks.mistakes: Treating a half-day workshop as the whole engagement · skipping Discover.
blocks.handoff: → choose learning route (Format A or B).
blocks.example: WORK: Northbridge runs 02 → 06 over about 12 weeks; the half-day workshop is one day inside 05. [fictional]

var.PLAY: Riverside fits around the fixture calendar.
var.HEAL: St Aldric adds clinical review gates.

blocks.prompt: Generic Claude prompt: 'Sort these activities into the six campus sections and explain each placement in one line.'
blocks.verify: Placement against the six-section taxonomy on Start Here.
blocks.fallback: Card sort on the Start Here process strip.
blocks.l_obj: Sort 10 activity cards into the six sections.
blocks.explain: Diverge to explore, converge to decide — twice: first on the problem, then on the solution.

exercise.situation: 10 activity cards (e.g. 'site visit', 'value proposition', 'proposal').
questions: Place each in a section.
Which happen before the workshop?
Which need user evidence?

answer_key.sample_answer: Proposal 02; site visit 03; journey 04; idea sheet 05; value proposition 06; test 06.X3.
answer_key.success_criteria: ≥ 8/10 correctly placed.

Use the OS agent with real context
Decide what stays — a human decision

What do you do?
What must a human decide?

blocks.name: Intro to CoDesign & Proposal
blocks.sub: Before the Double Diamond · project framing
blocks.obj: Explain what CoDesign brings, understand the client's real challenge and turn it into a clear, tailored proposal.
blocks.who: Business/Sales brings the opportunity and commercial ambition · CoDesign team challenges the brief, selects the approach and writes the proposal · Client shares context, constraints and expected outcomes.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead (N3) signs off the proposal; account owner validates commercial terms.
blocks.when: At the start of an opportunity, before the project is launched and before Discover. Prerequisite: 02.03 Client Intelligence brief.
blocks.inputs: Client brief or request; business context; stakeholders, timing, budget if known; relevant previous work. Minimum evidence: a named sponsor and a written brief (even an email).
steps: Understand the initial request and context
Reframe: challenge the problem as stated
blocks.output: A tailored proposal: challenge, objectives, approach, phases, activities, deliverables, stakeholders, timeline and budget.
blocks.std: A non-designer can read it and explain what will happen, why, and what the client receives.
blocks.quality: Client-specific, outcome-oriented, realistic; the method answers a real need.
blocks.mistakes: Selling a workshop when the problem needs research · copying a past proposal without reframing · promising outcomes that need user evidence.
blocks.handoff: Proposal accepted and a sponsor named → 03.01 Kick-off & Planning.
blocks.example: WORK: Northbridge asks for 'a workshop to fix the restaurant'. The team reframes it as 'make the anchor day worth the commute' and proposes Discover (3 weeks), a half-day Format A workshop and a test plan. [fictional]

var.PLAY: Riverside asks for 'faster kiosks'. Reframe around the half-time journey, including access needs.
var.HEAL: St Aldric asks for 'a new menu'. Reframe around choice timing and family involvement; flag clinical sign-off in scope.
var.LEARN: Lakeshore asks for 'cheaper meal plans'. Reframe around the commuter's 3-hour gap.

blocks.cred: Choose 2-3 from 02.02. Credential grid S06 slide 7 proves projects are referenced, not their impact.
blocks.tools: Proposal template · Double Diamond overview · Miro · PowerPoint
blocks.deck: [S03, slides 6-9] · [S05, slides 27-28] planning and 70/20/10 · [S06, slide 5] engagement triggers
blocks.prompt: Use Brief Challenger with the client email and Client Intelligence brief: 'Score this brief on readiness, list the 5 clarification questions to ask before quoting, and flag any walk-away signals.'
blocks.verify: Scope, price, dates and named credentials; remove any figure the client has not given.
blocks.fallback: Fill the proposal template section by section: Context → Why now → Challenge → Objectives → Approach → Activities → Deliverables → Timeline → Team.
blocks.l_obj: Reframe a client request into a CoDesign challenge statement and justify the proposed approach.
blocks.explain: Presales is not Discover. Its job is to decide what deserves to be explored and how.

templates.label: XP Design for Client — proposal template (SharePoint)

exercise.situation: A client asks for 'a one-day workshop to redesign our staff canteen menu'. Budget set, date booked.
questions: What is the client really asking for, and what might the real challenge be?
Which two questions would you ask before agreeing?
Would you propose the workshop as requested? If not, what instead, and how do you justify it commercially?

answer_key.sample_answer: Real challenge is likely participation or experience, not the menu. Questions: 'What would success look like in 6 months?' and 'What do you already know about why people do or do not use the canteen?'. Keep the date but propose 2-3 weeks of light Discover before it, so the workshop works on evidence.
answer_key.success_criteria: Challenge statement names a user, a moment and an outcome; justification links approach to risk avoided.

blocks.name: Credentials Examples
blocks.obj: Select the few credentials that prove we can solve this client's challenge.
blocks.who: Business/Sales shares the opportunity · CoDesign team selects and adapts the story · Client reacts to what resonates.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead checks every claim against the credential source and confidentiality rules.
blocks.when: During Presales, once the challenge is understood.
blocks.inputs: Client context and challenge; credential library; previous deliverables. Minimum evidence: each credential has an approved source file.
steps: Understand what needs to be proven
Adapt the story to the client
blocks.output: A short tailored selection: challenge, approach, outputs and, where documented, impact.
blocks.std: Every proof point traces to an approved document; confidential details removed.
blocks.quality: Relevant over exhaustive, recent, visual, connected to the client's challenge.
blocks.mistakes: Showing 15 logos · quoting impact figures nobody can source · using a confidential client name without approval.
blocks.example: HEAL: for St Aldric, shortlist Clariane (dining model, care homes) and explain the transfer limits: care homes are not acute wards, so lead with the method and the resident journey, not the numbers. [credential listed in S06; impact figures to verify]

var.WORK: Microsoft and Santander for workplace dining; show the persona and roadmap outputs.
var.PLAY: Arsenal FC or Roland-Garros for matchday F&B; check which artifacts are approved.
var.LEARN: No verified education credential: use a cross-sector case and say so openly.

blocks.cred: A listing proves a project is referenced; it does not prove a deliverable or quantified impact exists.
blocks.prompt: No selection agent exists. Generic Claude prompt: 'From this credential list [paste], shortlist 3 for a [segment] client whose challenge is [x]. For each: why it is relevant, the one proof point to lead with, and what must be verified before use.'
blocks.verify: Every figure and client name against SharePoint; sharing permission.
blocks.fallback: Filter the credential grid by segment and challenge, then apply the 3 questions: relevant? sourced? shareable?
blocks.l_obj: Shortlist 3 credentials with an explicit relevance rationale and one sourced proof point each.
blocks.explain: Don't show everything we have done. Show what proves we can solve this client's challenge.

exercise.situation: You are pitching to a hospital group that wants to improve the patient meal experience. The library holds 40 credentials.
questions: On which criteria do you shortlist three?
Your strongest case is an airport lounge. Do you show it, and how?
For your best credential, which single proof point do you lead with?

answer_key.sample_answer: Criteria: similar user moment, similar constraint (safety, time), approved artifacts. Show the lounge as 'how we redesign a time-pressured service moment', not as a sector match. Lead with a method proof (journey + pilot) unless an impact figure is sourced.
answer_key.success_criteria: Shortlist justified on user moment and constraint, not on sector logo alone.

blocks.name: Client Intelligence
blocks.obj: Understand the client's context, priorities, stakeholders and signals before engaging further.
blocks.who: Business/Sales shares account knowledge · CoDesign team researches and formulates hypotheses · Internal experts add sector knowledge.
blocks.acc: Account owner validates facts; CoDesign lead validates hypotheses.
blocks.when: At the very start of Presales, before or alongside first meetings.
blocks.inputs: Account information, previous proposals, public reports, CRM notes. Minimum evidence: sources listed for every fact.
blocks.output: A concise Client Intelligence Brief: context, priorities, challenges, stakeholders, signals, hypotheses, questions to validate.
blocks.std: Facts and assumptions are visibly separated; 3 questions ready for the first meeting.
blocks.quality: Relevant, recent, actionable; analysis produces better questions.
blocks.mistakes: A 30-page dossier nobody reads · presenting assumptions as facts · skipping the account team.
blocks.handoff: Brief shared with Sales and used in 02.01.
blocks.example: WORK: Northbridge annual report mentions 'return-to-office cost discipline' [fictional]. Fact: real-estate budget frozen. Assumption: employees dislike the restaurant. Question: 'What would make Tuesday worth coming in for?'

var.PLAY: Riverside: season-ticket renewal rate, new stand opening, local transport works.
var.HEAL: St Aldric: patient experience scores, waste targets, nurse staffing pressure.
var.LEARN: Lakeshore: enrolment trends, commuter ratio, affordability commitments.

blocks.cred: Previous work with the same client or sector (search 02.02 library).
blocks.tools: Account documentation, annual reports, CRM/SharePoint, stakeholder map
blocks.prompt: 'Prepare a pre-Discovery briefing on [client] for a first meeting with [role]. Separate [EVIDENCE] from [ASSUMPTION], list stakeholders and 3 questions to ask.'
blocks.verify: Every fact has a source; nothing confidential from CRM pasted into external tools beyond approved use.
blocks.fallback: Use the 9-heading template: Who → Context → Priorities → Challenges → Stakeholders → Trends → Relationship → Opportunities → Questions.
blocks.l_obj: Sort statements into facts and assumptions and write 3 open meeting questions.
blocks.explain: Client Intelligence is not Discovery. It prepares Discovery.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — Client Intelligence brief template: MISSING, owner Gabriel

exercise.situation: You have 45 minutes to prepare a first meeting with the Head of Workplace of a global bank.
questions: Where do you look first, and for what?
Sort: they are cutting real-estate costs · employees dislike the current offer · the CEO mentioned hybrid work in the annual report.
Write the three questions you would ask.

answer_key.sample_answer: Fact: CEO mention in annual report (sourced). Assumptions: cost cutting (unless sourced), employee dislike (needs evidence). Good questions are open and about outcomes: 'What does a good office day look like for you?'
answer_key.success_criteria: Correct fact/assumption sort with a reason; questions are open, not leading.

blocks.name: Kick-off & Planning
blocks.obj: Launch the project, align everyone on challenge, scope and roles, and turn the proposal into a Discovery plan.
blocks.who: CoDesign team prepares and facilitates · Client project team shares context and constraints · Account team ensures continuity with Presales.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead owns the plan; client sponsor approves scope and governance.
blocks.when: Right after project confirmation, before any research.
blocks.inputs: Signed proposal, Client Intelligence, existing data, stakeholder list, timeline. Minimum evidence: named sponsor, decision owner and dates.
blocks.output: A shared Project & Discovery Plan with RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed).
blocks.std: Every research question has an activity, an owner and a date.
blocks.quality: Explicit scope and roles; learning-focused plan; realistic activities.
blocks.mistakes: Presenting conclusions at kick-off · no decision owner · research questions that are really solutions.
blocks.example: HEAL: St Aldric kick-off lists known (waste audit) vs unknown (why families feel excluded); research questions lead to ward shadowing and family interviews; RACI names the dietitian as Consulted for every concept. [fictional]

var.WORK: Northbridge: research questions on anchor-day behaviour; badge data owner named.
var.PLAY: Riverside: matchday observation slots booked around fixtures.
var.LEARN: Lakeshore: timetable data request and student union as Consulted.

blocks.cred: Cincinnati Children's materials are internal working documents; confirm sharing rules before showing outside the team.
blocks.prompt: 'From this signed proposal [paste], draft the kick-off agenda, a Know / Don't know / Assume table and 6 research questions mapped to Discovery activities.'
blocks.verify: Dates, names, scope; remove any 'finding' the AI presents before research.
blocks.fallback: Use the 12-heading template: Context → Ambition → Challenge → Know/Don't know → Assumptions → Questions → Activities → Stakeholders → Roles → Governance → Timeline → Next steps.
blocks.l_obj: Reframe a kick-off from 'conclusions' to 'learning plan' and match 3 activities to questions.
blocks.explain: Presales says what we propose to do; Kick-off turns it into how we will actually do it.

exercise.situation: The proposal is signed. The client team arrives expecting you to present conclusions.
questions: How do you reframe the session in the first five minutes?
List what is known and what must be learned.
Which three Discovery activities would you choose, and what does each answer?

answer_key.sample_answer: Open with the ambition and 'what we must learn to decide well'. Activities: observation (what people do), interviews (why), data review (how often). Each tied to one research question.
answer_key.success_criteria: Each activity answers a named question; nothing presented as a finding.

blocks.name: Research & Context Base
blocks.obj: Build a shared knowledge base before field research: what is known, assumed and missing.
blocks.who: CoDesign team collects and structures · Client provides data and documents · Account team adds history.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead reviews the fact/assumption split.
blocks.when: After kick-off, before interviews and visits.
blocks.inputs: Kick-off outputs, client studies, surveys, operational data, old personas/journeys. Minimum evidence: each fact cites a document and date.
blocks.output: A Context & Knowledge Base: facts, data, users, stakeholders, constraints, assumptions, gaps, questions.
blocks.std: Traceable to source; gaps written as research questions.
blocks.quality: Focused, evidence-based, connected to the challenge.
blocks.mistakes: Copying the whole survey · treating old personas as current · ignoring contradictions.
blocks.example: LEARN: Lakeshore's survey says 'affordable' is the top driver; the dashboard shows rising uptake of the cheapest item; the old persona says students 'want healthy options'. Contradiction flagged; question: 'What does affordable mean for a commuter on a work day?' [fictional]

var.WORK: Badge data vs 'nobody comes in on Mondays' assumption.
var.PLAY: Kiosk sales by minute vs complaints by stand.
var.HEAL: Plate-waste audit vs patient satisfaction comments.

blocks.prompt: Generic Claude prompt: 'Read these documents [attach]. Build a table Fact / Source / Date / Confidence, then list assumptions, contradictions and 5 research questions. Do not invent data.'
blocks.verify: Each fact against its source; no figure without a source.
blocks.fallback: Five questions on one Miro frame: What do we know? What evidence? What do we assume? What is missing? What do we investigate?
blocks.l_obj: Classify material into fact, assumption and contradiction, and convert the largest gap into a research question.
blocks.explain: Know what you know before you go into the field.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — 01_Discover folder; Context Base template: MISSING, owner Gabriel

exercise.situation: The client sends a 90-page satisfaction survey, two old personas and an operations dashboard.
questions: How do you decide what is worth keeping?
Give one fact, one assumption and one contradiction.
Turn the biggest gap into a research question.

answer_key.sample_answer: Keep what links to the challenge and is recent. A good research question is open and behavioural ('How do commuters decide where to eat between classes?').
answer_key.success_criteria: Fact cites source; research question is open and behavioural.

blocks.name: Visit & Interviews
blocks.obj: Understand real experience by combining what people say, what they do and what they experience.
blocks.who: CoDesign team researches and captures evidence · Client opens access to sites and people · Users and frontline staff share experience.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead approves guides and consent approach; client confirms site rules.
blocks.when: Once context and knowledge gaps are known.
blocks.inputs: Context Base, research questions, stakeholder map, guides, visit plan. Minimum evidence: at least 2 user types and 1 frontline role; consent recorded.
blocks.output: Field findings: observations, notes, quotes, behaviours, needs, pain points, workarounds, constraints, emerging insights.
blocks.std: Each finding is tagged observed / said / interpreted.
blocks.quality: Diverse perspectives; open, non-leading questions; real behaviour captured.
blocks.mistakes: Leading questions · only interviewing managers · mixing interpretation into notes · no consent.
blocks.handoff: Debriefed findings → 04.01 Personas and 04.02 Journey Map.
blocks.example: WORK: at Northbridge 12:30, observe that teams split into two queues and regroup at tables 15 min later (observed). Team lead says 'lunch is our team meeting' (said). Interpretation: the queue breaks the social moment. [fictional]

var.PLAY: Observe half-time from the concourse; interview a steward and a family.
var.HEAL: Shadow a ward host round; interview a family member with consent and ward approval.
var.LEARN: Observe the library annex at 13:00; interview commuters in the car park area.

blocks.cred: Cooper / Cincinnati site-visit playbook referenced on V1 board; confirm shareable version.
blocks.tools: Site Visit Playbook, interview guide, observation guide, Plaud/transcription, Miro
blocks.prompt: 'Draft a 45-minute interview guide for [user] on [research question]. Open questions only, with 2 follow-ups each, and an observation checklist for [site, time].'
blocks.verify: No leading questions; consent and anonymisation; transcripts are not pasted into tools without approval.
blocks.fallback: Paper guide: 5 open questions + 'tell me about the last time…' + observation grid (time, place, action, workaround).
blocks.l_obj: Rewrite leading questions and record observation, statement and interpretation separately.
blocks.explain: Don't only ask people what they need. Observe what they actually do.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — interview/observation guides and Site Visit Playbook: location TO CONFIRM (Cooper playbook requested in Diane's V1 comment)

exercise.situation: You are observing a staff restaurant at 12:30, with one hour on site and one interview slot with a frontline manager.
questions: What do you watch for that people would never tell you?
Rewrite: 'Don't you think the queue is too long?'
How do you record observation vs statement vs interpretation?

answer_key.sample_answer: Watch workarounds, waiting, who eats alone, trays left. Rewrite: 'Tell me about the last time you had lunch here.' Use three columns or tags: O / S / I.
answer_key.success_criteria: Rewritten question is open and neutral; notes are tagged O/S/I.

blocks.name: Benchmark
blocks.obj: Learn how others, inside and outside the sector, address similar challenges, and extract transferable principles.
blocks.who: CoDesign team researches and curates · Experts suggest references · Client reacts.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead checks sources and the 'so what' of each example.
blocks.when: In parallel with field research.
blocks.inputs: Research questions, themes, trend reports. Minimum evidence: every example has a source link and date.
blocks.output: A curated Benchmark & Inspiration Landscape with examples, principles and transferable learnings.
blocks.std: Each example answers 'so what for this client?'
blocks.quality: Focused, diverse, recent, sourced.
blocks.mistakes: A competitor list with no insight · copying features instead of principles · unsourced examples.
blocks.example: PLAY: to cut half-time queues, look at airport fast lanes and theme-park virtual queues; principle: 'move the wait out of the peak'. Benchmark is evidence from elsewhere, not proof it works here.

var.WORK: Co-working spaces' booking of team tables.
var.HEAL: Hotel room-service ordering windows.
var.LEARN: Public libraries that allow food zones.

blocks.tools: Benchmark agent, inspiration library, trend reports, web research
blocks.prompt: 'Find 8 examples (4 outside [sector]) addressing [challenge]. For each: what they do, why it works, transferable principle, source link and date. Flag anything you could not verify.'
blocks.verify: Open every link; check dates; remove examples without a live source.
blocks.fallback: Template row: Question → Theme → Example → What they do → Why it works → Principle → Transferability → Opportunity.
blocks.l_obj: Extract a transferable principle from an out-of-sector example and defend it to a sceptical client.
blocks.explain: Benchmark is not a collection of competitors. Always answer 'So what?'

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — Benchmark template: MISSING, owner Gabriel

exercise.situation: You need inspiration to reduce waiting time in a corporate restaurant.
questions: Name one example from outside food service and why.
What is the transferable principle, not the feature?
How do you answer 'but we are not a theme park'?

answer_key.sample_answer: E.g. airport security lanes: principle 'separate quick and complex transactions'. Answer: 'We are not copying the park, we are borrowing the idea of moving the wait.'
answer_key.success_criteria: Principle stated without the original feature; source named.

blocks.name: Personas
blocks.obj: Turn research findings into a few evidence-based user profiles built on behaviours, needs and pain points.
blocks.who: CoDesign team clusters research and drafts personas · Client challenges them · Users or frontline staff can validate.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead checks each trait against evidence.
blocks.when: After field research is debriefed.
blocks.inputs: Field findings, quotes, observations, data. Minimum evidence: each persona draws on at least 3 interviews or observations.
blocks.output: 2-4 personas: context, behaviours, goals, needs, motivations, pain points, quote, key journey moments, design implications.
blocks.std: Every trait links to evidence or is marked as an assumption.
blocks.quality: Behaviour-led, differentiated, actionable, not stereotypical.
blocks.mistakes: Demographic personas ('Sophie, 34, loves yoga') · invented quotes · too many personas.
blocks.example: HEAL: 'Ruth, the worried visitor' is defined by behaviour (visits at lunch, asks nurses whether Dad ate) and need (to know and help), not by age. Quote is from interview F02 [fictional dataset].

var.WORK: Maya, the anchor-day coordinator.

blocks.cred: Eli Lilly persona examples cited in S05 slide 25 ('Night-shift Marie') — confirm approved artifact.
blocks.prompt: 'From this interview synthesis [paste], propose 3 behaviour-based personas. For each trait cite the evidence ID or tag [ASSUMPTION]. No invented quotes.'
blocks.verify: Trait-to-evidence links; remove stereotypes and any quote not in transcripts.
blocks.fallback: Cluster stickies by behaviour on Miro, name each cluster with a verb phrase, fill the 11-field template.
blocks.l_obj: Rewrite a demographic persona into a behaviour-based one with evidence for each trait.
blocks.explain: A persona is discovered, not invented.

exercise.situation: Your team proposes: 'Sophie, 34, marketing manager, loves yoga and healthy food.'
questions: What is wrong with this persona?
Which evidence would you need to keep or drop each trait?
Rewrite it around a behaviour.

answer_key.sample_answer: It is demographic and unsourced; traits do not change design decisions. Rewrite: 'The 15-minute luncher: eats at her desk on meeting-heavy days, wants food she can trust without queuing.'
answer_key.success_criteria: Persona named by behaviour; each trait tagged evidence or assumption.

blocks.name: Journey Map
blocks.obj: Show the end-to-end experience across key moments, to understand what users do, think, feel and need, and where it breaks.
blocks.who: CoDesign team synthesises research, structures the journey and facilitates validation · Client/project team brings operational knowledge and challenges the map · Users and frontline staff provide the evidence and can validate key moments.
blocks.acc: CoDesign lead (N2+) signs off that every pain point carries evidence.
blocks.when: During Define, once personas and research findings exist. After or alongside 04.01, before How Might We questions and workshop challenges.
blocks.inputs: Personas; interview findings, observations, quotes; existing processes; touchpoints; Context Base; operational data. Minimum evidence: each stage supported by at least one observation or interview; each pain point by 2+ sources or marked [TO VALIDATE].
steps: Define the persona and the journey scope (start and end)
Identify 5-7 stages from the user's point of view
Map actions and touchpoints (physical, human, digital, printed)
Extract opportunity areas and How Might We questions

WORK.users: Hybrid employees, team leads, visitors, front-of-house and restaurant staff.
WORK.constraints: Real-estate budget frozen; restaurant contract renewal in 16 months; union consultation for any change to service hours.
evidence: Badge data: Tuesday-Thursday peaks at 78% of desks, Monday and Friday below 30% [fictional]
Restaurant queue observed at 12:20-12:45: median wait 11 min [fictional observation]

Service desk: 34% of tickets are room booking or 'cannot find a quiet space' [fictional]

Lunch is the main social anchor but the queue breaks the team moment
Quiet space is the missing ingredient on peak days
hmw: How might we make the team lunch a 20-minute moment instead of a 45-minute logistics task?
How might we help a team lead plan an anchor day in two minutes?
